articles.title: Bares de Santos podem ser obrigados a destruir garrafas vazias | G1
articles.standfirst: Proposta está em análise na Câmara Municipal de Santos. Proposta busca dificultar a falsificação de bebidas e cita casos de contaminação por metanol registrados em 2025.
articles.summary: A falsificação de bebidas em Santos motiva projeto que prevê multas e cassação de alvará para bares que não destruírem garrafas vazias após o consumo.
articles.body:
bebidas alcóolicas álcool garrafas bar drinks — Foto: Pexels

Um projeto de lei em Santos , no litoral de São Paulo, quer obrigar os comércios a destruírem garrafas vazias para evitar que sejam reutilizadas na falsificação de bebidas alcóolicas. A proposta será discutida na Câmara Municipal nesta terça-feira (13).

A proposta integra a restrição ao Código de Posturas da cidade, estabelecendo que bares, restaurantes, casas noturnas, lanchonetes, adegas e outros estabelecimentos comerciais destruam ou danifiquem as embalagens após o consumo.

O texto, de autoria do vereador Cacá Teixeira (PSDB), prevê a medida por meio de quebra, corte do gargalo, amassamento, perfuração ou trituração, entre outros métodos autorizados que impeçam o reaproveitamento.

O projeto também proíbe a venda, doação ou cessão das garrafas vazias a terceiros, exceto para reciclagem por meio de pontos de descarte públicos, cooperativas ou empresas autorizadas, e programas regulamentados de logística reversa.

Ainda está previsto no projeto que o descumprimento poderá resultar em advertência na primeira infração, multas em caso de reincidência e até suspensão e cassação do alvará de funcionamento em casos mais graves.

De acordo com o vereador, a proposta foi apresentada para dificultar os crimes de falsificação de bebidas. Ele ainda citou os casos envolvendo contaminação com metanol em 2025, que causaram graves problemas de saúde aos consumidores.

Além do Código de Posturas, a fiscalização deveria ficar a cargo da Vigilância Sanitária e dos órgãos de defesa do consumidor. Caso a proposta seja aprovada definitivamente, sancionada e publicada, a regra deverá entrar em vigor após 90 dias.

articles.title: French supermarkets face millions in losses after cyberattack hits refrigerators nationwide
articles.summary: Hackers targeted Danfoss refrigerator controls across French supermarkets, forcing chains like Carrefour and Monoprix to discard massive food stocks.
articles.body: A cyberattack in France forced multiple grocery stores to discard large amounts of temperature-sensitive product after hackers turned the heat up on food refrigerators in hundreds of stores across at least five chain brands. The hack, according to Reuters and European officials, affected chains such as Carrefour, Monoprix, Les Mousquetaires, E. Leclerc and Coopérative U. The CEO of Coopérative U, a retail group structured as a cooperative of independently owned businesses, confirmed the cyberattack in a Monday post on X. "I confirm that a cyberattack has been affecting, since last night, the cold production facilities of several stores in our network Coopérative U," he wrote in the post. FOREIGN HACKERS BREACH TWO MORE US WATER UTILITIES, THREATEN SAFETY OF COLORADO RESIDENTS "Our teams are fully mobilized, in coordination with refrigeration specialists, to restore the situation as quickly as possible. An investigation will be necessary to shed full light on this attack. Targeting equipment essential to the preservation of fresh products and to the food supply of the French people is of extreme gravity and is unprecedented. It is unacceptable," he concluded. IF HACKERS CRIPPLE AMERICA'S WATER, THE CONSEQUENCES COULD BE CATASTROPHIC The Paris prosecutor's office also confirmed the cyberattack, characterizing it as a "large-scale" attack that affected "connected refrigerators in several major food retailers across France." Carrefour said roughly 80 of its stores were affected while Monoprix, which operates 490 stores in France according to Reuters, said 5% of its stores were affected. IRAN-LINKED HACKERS SUSPECTED IN UK POWER-PLANT SHUTDOWN AFTER ALLEGED MINNESOTA WATER ATTACK Les Mousquetaires said fridges at approximately 150 of its stores were heated up to 50 degrees Celsius (122 degrees Fahrenheit) for six hours. A company spokesperson also said all affected food had been discarded, according to Reuters. While the incident's financial toll on the supermarket has yet to be officially tabulated, experts estimated the losses to be upwards of 10 million euros, equivalent to roughly $11.2 million. INVESTIGATORS BELIEVE IRANIAN HACKERS ARE LIKELY BEHIND CYBERATTACK ON MINNESOTA WATER SYSTEMS: REPORT The attack likely resulted in the loss of "tens of millions of euros nationwide in a single day," Intermarche CEO Thierry Cotillard said during a televised interview in France, according to Reuters. A source with knowledge of the refrigerator systems reportedly told AFP that the hackers targeted refrigerator controls systems from Danish manufacturer Danfoss. CHINESE HACKERS TARGET NASA AND KEY US AGENCIES, DOJ ALLEGES Danfoss, in turn, told AFP that most of the affected equipment were "legacy" products which "no longer receive software or security updates." The company also added that some of the systems affected were using "outdated firmware" which it had long-counseled its purchasers to update. Danfoss did not immediately respond to Fox News Digital's request for further comment. TRUMP PLAN TAPS US FIRMS TO FIGHT FOREIGN CYBERCRIME French Prime Minister Sebastien Lecornu has instructed France's National Cyber security Agency (ANSSI) to conduct an investigation. ANSSI has already identified "a vulnerability in software supplied by a Danish company and has contacted the vendor," a source close to Lecornu reportedly told AFP. Christophe Hansen, the European Union's Commissioner for Agriculture and Food, denounced the attack as an affront on European food safety. IRANIAN HACKERS ATTACKED OUR WATER SYSTEMS. HERE ARE 5 THINGS OUR LEADERS NEED TO DO NOW "I strongly condemn the cyberattack targeting food products at Intermarche, Cooperative U, Leclerc. Food security requires more attention at all levels. Because the weaponization of food has become a reality," he said in a Monday post on X. CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP Fox News Digital contacted the Paris Prosecutor's Office, Carrefour, Monoprix, E. Leclerc, Les Mousquetaires and Coopérative U for confirmation and additional comment. Reuters contributed to this report.

articles.title: Amid AI push, no internet in 48% of Karnataka schools
articles.summary: Karnataka’s AI-in-schools push faces a digital divide: UDISE+ 2025-26 shows 48% of 74,578 schools lack internet, worst in South India.
articles.body: BENGALURU: While Karnataka is favouring introduction of AI skills and coding in its schools, nearly 48% of the state’s 74,578 schools do not have internet connectivity, exposing a glaring digital divide.According to UDISE+ report released by Union ministry of education for 2025–26, the state’s connectivity rate is well below the national average of 67%. Nearly one in three schools in India lacks internet access, while every second school in Karnataka lacks the facility.Home to the country’s IT capital, Karnataka has the highest percentage of schools without internet connectivity among the southern states — both as a proportion of total schools and in absolute numbers.The gap is particularly alarming in government schools. Of the state’s 48,527 government-managed schools, only 18,007 have internet facilities, leaving about 30,520 (63%) without connectivity.These contrasting figures come at a time when chief minister DK Shivakumar, during his Independence Day, announced the AI Akshara Abhiyana and Coding Gurukula initiatives across Karnataka, aimed at introducing AI education in schools from Class 6.Subsequently, the CM said AI training had already begun for Class 9 students in govt schools and directed officials to explore extending it to younger students, with support from the information technology department and private organisations. However, the widening infrastructure gap raises questions about how uniformly these initiatives can be implemented across the state.D Shashi Kumar, general secretary of the Associated Managements of Primary and Secondary Schools in Karnataka (KAMS), pointed out that the digital divide could widen if the number of schools with functional internet connections were considered, as several schools reporting internet access do not have an active connection.“AI education requires access to computers, suitable software, trained teachers and, for many learning applications, reliable internet connectivity. Without these basic facilities, students in poorly connected schools risk being left behind even as their peers gain exposure to emerging technologies. Although the government has pinned its hopes on CSR initiatives, how many schools will these initiatives cover? All these programmes require substantial financial resources. Will the government be able to provide the necessary funds?” he asked.Karnataka’s performance is also poor compared with that of its southern neighbours. Andhra Pradesh has internet access in 99.2% of its 60,843 schools, while Tamil Nadu has achieved 99% coverage across 57,566 schools. Kerala reports connectivity in 92.6% of its 15,750 schools. Telangana, despite having a sizeable gap of its own, has internet access in 76.5% of its 41,762 schools. Karnataka, with connectivity in just 51.7% of its schools, has the lowest coverage in South India, the report revealed.“The proportion of schools without internet connectivity in Karnataka is more than twice that of Telangana, where 23.5% of schools lack access, and over six times the national average of 32.6%,” a Bengaluru-based academician said.Nationally, 4.77 lakh of India’s 14.67 lakh schools lack internet access, according to the report. articles.title: US hits Bank of America with $1.2 billion fine, saying it violated money laundering, sanctions laws
articles.summary: Treasury Department said Tuesday that it’s imposing $1.2 billion in fines on Bank of America for allegedly violating anti-money laundering and sanctions laws...
articles.body:
WASHINGTON (AP) — The U.S. Treasury Department said Tuesday that it's imposing $1.2 billion in fines on Bank of America for allegedly violating anti-money laundering and sanctions laws.

The fines on America's second-biggest bank amount to the third-largest in the department's history.

"When a bank of this size fails to meet its anti-money laundering and sanctions obligations, the consequences extend far beyond its own walls, exposing the entire U.S. financial system to significant illicit finance risks," Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent said in a statement. "Today's actions send a clear message that even the biggest financial institutions are not above the law."

Treasury said Bank of America also reached an $11.6 million settlement with the department's Office of Foreign Assets Control over "apparent violations of numerous sanctions programs, including on Iran, Russia, narcotics, and global terrorism."

In a statement, Treasury said its Financial Crimes Enforcement Network (FinCEN) assessed the $1.2 billion penalty for Bank of America's "failure to mitigate and report priority national security risks, including Chinese Money Laundering Networks and illicit finance along the southwest border.''

The penalty includes $750 million that will go to the U.S. Office of the Comptroller of the Currency, the largest fine ever imposed by that federal bank regulatory agency.

Treasury said that Bank of America "admits that it willfully violated'' the 1970 Bank Secrecy Act, which requires banks to help the government detect and prevent money laundering.

"Financial crime compliance is serious, and we are responsible for getting it right,'' Bank of America said in a statement. "We worked with regulators to reach these penalty resolutions stemming from violations cited in the previously reported 2024 (Comptroller of the Currency) Consent Order and FinCEN's investigation.

" We have invested billions of dollars in technology and dedicated thousands of employees to combat financial crime, and our team is far along with and committed to completing the work required to address the issues raised by our regulators.''

The latest action is the third-largest penalty ever issued by the Treasury Department, behind a roughly $4 billion settlement in 2023 with Binance, the world's largest cryptocurrency exchange, and an approximately $3 billion settlement with Canada-based TD Bank the following year. Both those historic actions happened as part of the Biden administration's focus on anti-money laundering and efforts to promote compliance with the then-emerging virtual currency industry.

articles.title: Poll: 43 percent support ‘Medicare for all’
articles.summary: Nearly 43 percent of Americans support the idea of “Medicare for all,” according to an Axios/Ipsos poll released Tuesday, as concerns over health costs mount ahead of the midterm elections. People who said they support Medicare for all outnumbered its opponents by a nearly 2-to-1 margin, while a bipartisan majority of Americans said they think the…
articles.body:
Nearly 43 percent of Americans support the idea of “Medicare for all,” according to an Axios/Ipsos poll released Tuesday, as concerns over health costs mount ahead of the midterm elections.

People who said they support Medicare for all outnumbered its opponents by a nearly 2-to-1 margin, while a bipartisan majority of Americans said they think the federal government should be willing to spend more tax dollars to lower healthcare costs.

While respondents said they support federal involvement, they are losing trust in the government.

Roughly half of respondents said they have a “great deal or a fair amount of trust” in information about health topics from the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC), down from 62 percent in March 2025.

Less than 20 percent of Americans said they trust information about health topics from President Trump, while just 25 percent said they trust Secretary of Health and Human Services (HHS) Robert F. Kennedy Jr.

Congress also got low scores, with 25 percent saying they trust Democrats in Congress on health topics, while 20 percent said they trust Republicans.

Like most polls about Medicare for all, the support was very partisan. More than 60 percent of Democrats said they support a program that would provide government-run health insurance to all Americans, largely replacing private health insurance. Just under half of independents said the same, while a majority of Republicans said they are opposed.

Medicare for all has been a slogan for progressive Democrats in previous campaigns, most notably when Sen. Bernie Sanders (I-Vt.) ran for president in 2016 as well as the 2020 Democratic presidential primary.

But amid crushing health costs, the latest findings show that there could be an opening for progressive Democrats campaigning on the idea to win over some swing-state voters.

A KFF survey last week found about two-thirds of Americans said they support the idea of Medicare for all, the highest share since the organization began polling on the idea 10 years ago.

Yet, many people don’t know how to define Medicare for all, and the KFF poll showed support changed when people were presented with arguments for and against. A national debate would likely include more details about costs and tradeoffs that aren’t being captured in surface-level campaign slogans.

The KFF survey found support declined when people heard the arguments that Medicare for all could lead to delays in medical tests and treatments and tax increases or threaten the current Medicare program. But support grew when respondents heard that a national insurance plan could make health insurance “a right” or eliminate premiums and cost-sharing.

According to the Axios poll, opponents said the top reason they do not support Medicare for All is a fear of a worse quality of care than private insurance, followed by feeling the program would be too expensive for taxpayers.

The Axios/Ipsos poll is based on a nationally representative probability sample of 1,122 general population adults age 18 or older.

The margin of error is plus or minus 3 percentage points

articles.title: Boston Fed's Collins wants to raise rates 'a bit more' before the end of the year
articles.summary: Boston Federal Reserve president Susan Collins suggested Tuesday that she favors raising interest rates again this year to combat inflation.
articles.body:
Boston Federal Reserve president Susan Collins suggested Tuesday that she favors raising interest rates again this year to combat inflation.

"I … currently expect that it will be appropriate to raise rates a bit further before the end of the year to ensure a timely and durable return of inflation to the Committee's 2% target," Collins said in a speech in Boston. "However, my view of the need for further policy action, and the appropriate timing, will depend importantly on how the totality of incoming data shapes my outlook and the associated balance of risks."

Collins noted that inflation on a three-month annualized basis as measured by the Personal Consumption Expenditures index, excluding volatile food and energy, was only 2%. But she expects total and core inflation to again run above the Fed's 2% target in the coming months, given the r ecent jump in prices of refined energy products like jet and diesel fuel, as well as home heating oil.

Collins expects these price increases will keep inflation elevated in the transportation sector, lodging and related services —where energy is an important input — as well as in materials used to build data centers.

"Against this backdrop, it will be important to monitor whether elevated inflation remains largely confined to energy and AI build-out-related categories, while price growth continues to moderate elsewhere — or whether evidence of price pressures broadens," said Collins.

Collins' comments come ahead of a fresh reading on inflation as measured by the Consumer Price Index due out Wednesday. Economists expect CPI rose 3.6% in September. Excluding volatile food and energy, prices are expected to have risen 2.5%, or 0.2% month over month.

Elsewhere Tuesday, New York Federal Reserve president John Williams told Bloomberg he still sees one more interest rate hike as appropriate this year, but at the moment he doesn't believe it will be necessary for the central bank to increase rates again in 2027.

Markets are betting the Fed will hold rates steady at the end of the month, but raise again in December.

Jennifer Schonberger is a veteran financial journalist covering markets, the economy, and investing. At Yahoo Finance, she covers the Federal Reserve, Congress, the White House, the Treasury, the SEC, the economy, cryptocurrencies, and the intersection of Washington policy with finance. Follow her on X @Jenniferisms and on Instagram .

articles.title: Trump Threatens CEOs as Tactic Against Allies, Ex-Finance Minister Says
articles.summary: US President Donald Trump’s administration privately pressures foreign CEOs and business leaders to bring their governments into line with the White House’s...
articles.body:
(Bloomberg) -- US President Donald Trump's administration privately pressures foreign CEOs and business leaders to bring their governments into line with the White House's demands, Canada's former deputy prime minister says in a new memoir.

"The Trump team is swaggeringly, rudely aggressive, even behind closed doors," writes Chrystia Freeland, who also served as finance minister, foreign minister and trade minister during Justin Trudeau's nine years in power. "Trump's cabinet secretaries miss no opportunity to warn foreign CEOs of the dire consequences if their leaders don't fall in line."

The book is titled Unreliable Boyfriend: An Insider's View of Dealing with a Chaotic Superpower, Plutocrats, and Other Complicated People. It combines behind-the-scenes accounts of her dealings with Trump and other US officials with a retelling of her dramatic split from Trudeau in December 2024.

The book's central argument is that America's allies have too often rewarded Trump's bullying with concessions that fail to produce results. Freeland makes it clear she was frustrated with people who complained privately but capitulated to Trump publicly — and warns that China is gaining greater power as a result of US policies.

"Too often today, America's allies perform the Trump-era equivalent of woke virtue signaling — too many of us talk tough about the United States, but carry a small stick. Too much is at stake for that sort of quisling behavior," Freeland writes.

She praises Prime Minister Mark Carney, her longtime friend, in whose cabinet she served for several months before her exit from politics. But she criticizes the government's decision in June 2025 to drop a digital services tax that would have affected US tech firms, only for Trump to hike tariffs on Canadian goods weeks later anyway.

While the most visible fight between the US and its allies is over tariffs, "the more consequential battle may be over Washington's insistence that Big Tech be allowed to operate freely around the world without being meaningfully taxed or policed," she writes.

The administration brings its demands directly to foreign business leaders. After Carney's famous "middle powers" speech at the World Economic Forum in Davos in January, Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent hosted a dinner with business executives. One guest at that event later delivered a stark message to Freeland, according to her.

articles.title: Saudi national arrested after allegedly hiding recording device in OpenAI office
articles.summary: An OpenAI employee from Saudi Arabia has been arrested after allegedly hiding a recording device in the company’s offices, the Department of Justice (DOJ) said Tuesday. Abdulrahman Alfozan, a 35-year-old Saudi national who had worked as an engineer at OpenAI since last July, was charged with using or attempting to use a device to intercept…
articles.body:
An OpenAI employee from Saudi Arabia has been arrested after allegedly hiding a recording device in the company’s offices, the Department of Justice (DOJ) said Tuesday.

Abdulrahman Alfozan, a 35-year-old Saudi national who had worked as an engineer at OpenAI since last July, was charged with using or attempting to use a device to intercept oral communications.

The recording device was discovered at one of the firm’s San Francisco offices in late September, according to the DOJ. It was plugged into a USB port on the back of a television in an executive conference room and covered in toilet paper.

“We used our models to understand the device and where it had come from, identifying that a specific employee had planted it a few days earlier,” OpenAI said in a post on the social platform X.

“We referred the matter to the FBI, and we’re grateful to the agents and prosecutors who moved quickly to make an arrest,” they continued. “The FBI’s investigation is ongoing and we will continue to support their work.”

In the days before the device was found, video surveillance footage showed Alfozan near the conference room, despite having no authority to access or participate in meetings there, the DOJ said.

He also allegedly asked a productivity tool about OpenAI’s building addresses, meeting rooms, calendars and the locations of executives, while a chatbot linked to Alfozan’s spouse inquired about building, installing and remotely accessing a device.

OpenAI security personnel found another recording device when they searched Alfozan’s bag earlier this month.

The company said they currently have “no indications of this individual inappropriately accessing or exfiltrating model weights, source code, or customer data.” They also noted that the employee was fired.

“The Bay Area and Silicon Valley lead the world in developing tomorrow’s technology, and our Office will continue to stand at the forefront of protecting that American innovation,” Craig Missakian, U.S. attorney for the Northern District of California, said in a statement. “For us it is a matter of national security.”

articles.title: Federal energy regulators shoot down grid operator’s plan to cut power to data centers during shortfalls
articles.summary: The nation’s energy regulators have shot down a bid from a regional grid operator to cut power to some large data centers during a supply shortfall — leaving the issue largely in the hands of states. Regional grid operator PJM, which manages the electric grid for several East Coast and Midwest states, proposed an ability…
articles.body:
The nation’s energy regulators have shot down a bid from a regional grid operator to cut power to some large data centers during a supply shortfall — leaving the issue largely in the hands of states.

Regional grid operator PJM, which manages the electric grid for several East Coast and Midwest states, proposed an ability to cut power to new large consumers when it’s facing a shortage.

Its proposal would have applied to large data centers that don’t bring their own power sources.

However, the Federal Energy Regulatory Commission (FERC) rejected PM’s proposal, saying it may violate the Federal Power Act.

The commissioners wrote that the law “leaves to the states alone ‘any other sale’ — most notably any retail sale” of electricity.

The ruling comes after bipartisan governors and the Trump administration pushed PJM to do more to address rising electricity prices, in which data centers’ massive electricity demand is a factor.

Jeff Dennis, senior counsel at consulting firm Co2efficient, said that the decision puts pressure on states to set their own policy. Dennis, a former FERC staffer, said that the policies that states put in place could differ significantly.

He said that “adds to the number of things that the states and that PJM and to some degree, still FERC, have to sort out” to avoid high power prices and blackouts in the future.

PJM spokesperson Jeff Shields said in an email that the grid operator is “reviewing the Commission’s order with an eye toward how we can fulfill FERC’s requirements while recognizing the responsibilities FERC indicated belong to the states and honoring the concept that existing electricity customers should not be unfairly burdened by new, energy intensive customers in the form of higher costs or decreased reliability.”

articles.title: Elon Musk just gave $276M to help the GOP win mid-term elections. For a trillionaire, that’s like you spending about $60
articles.summary: Musk’s plans to establish a third American political party that would rival the GOP appear to be behind him.
articles.body:
Just over a year ago, Elon Musk's relationship with Donald Trump had broken down to the point that the former briefly weighed establishing a third American political party.

That no longer appears to be the case, as Musk is now bankrolling Republican efforts to hang onto Congress in the hotly-contested November midterms. He's reportedly spent $276 million — a sum that would make him the largest private-sector donor in the 2026 midterm election cycle. Overall, Musk's political donations in 2025 and 2026 total $366 million , The New York Times reported.

The tax breaks in Trump's 'big beautiful bill' expire after 2028. Here are 4 moves to make before the window closes

Jeff Bezos backs a platform that lets anyone invest in rental homes for as little as $100 — 6 ways to build wealth like a landlord without actually being one

Dave Ramsey warns nearly 50% of Americans are making 1 big Social Security mistake. Here's what it is and 3 simple steps to fix it ASAP

Political groups are obligated to report their third-quarter spending commitments to the Federal Election Commission on Oct. 15.

The Times also reported that Musk is pouring political cash into key Senate races, along with efforts to reach Republican voters who are less likely to turn out when Trump's name isn't on the ballot.

Musk became the first trillionaire in history on the back of SpaceX's blockbuster initial public offering in June. He has at times lost trillionaire status due to sharp fluctuations in SpaceX's stock price, with Forbes reporting Musk's net worth at $982.9 billion as of Oct. 13.

This means Musk's reported $276 million midterm donation amounts to just 0.028% of his net worth. A new Federal Reserve survey of consumer finances showed that American households had a median net worth of $215,900 . With this in mind, a comparable donation size to Musk's — or 0.028% of the median net worth — amounts to about $60 for a typical U.S. household.

Moneywise reached out to Musk's representatives for comment but didn't hear back in time for publication.

Musk's midterm donation shows that the Tesla CEO hasn't lost his appetite for the national political arena. After last-year's public blow-up with Trump, Musk emphasized he'd like to return to tending to his business empire.

"In terms of political spending, I'm going to do a lot less in the future," he told CNBC in May 2025.

Yet Trump and Musk took steps to mend their fences, and Musk has since returned to Washington D.C. for high-profile state dinners, along with other tech-focused events at the White House. On Oct. 8, Musk attended Trump's AI summit alongside other tech titans, where he received the National Medal of Science from Trump.

articles.title: Global law enforcement agencies, tech firms disrupt West African scam network
articles.summary: A group of law enforcement agencies from around the world teamed up with a handful of high-profile technology firms to disrupt West African criminal scam networks, the Justice Department (DOJ) announced Tuesday. The operation led to “dozens” of arrests and 117 trafficking victims rescued from scam compounds in Ghana, the DOJ said. Authorities in the…
articles.body:
A group of law enforcement agencies from around the world teamed up with a handful of high-profile technology firms to disrupt West African criminal scam networks, the Justice Department (DOJ) announced Tuesday.

The operation led to “dozens” of arrests and 117 trafficking victims rescued from scam compounds in Ghana, the DOJ said . Authorities in the country seized hundreds of electronic devices, and at least $11 million was identified in potentially freezable funds

Teams with the DOJ, FBI and other U.S. federal agencies convened at the National Crime Agency (NCA) in London to exchange intelligence about a transnational criminal scam network with cybercrime authorities around the world, including those in Ghana and Nigeria.

Authorities teamed up with more than a dozen technology firms — such as Meta, OpenAI, Microsoft, Google, Starlink and Coinbase — to shut down linked accounts and stop active scams before they occurred.

Meta said in a blog post it removed more than 3.7 million accounts, pages or groups accused of targeting users in the U.S. and United Kingdom. Most of these profiles impersonated American and British users.

Microsoft suspended accounts suspected of being linked to the cybercrime, while Coinbase helped identify more than 65 victims and stopped more than $415,000 in potential scams, according to Meta.

“These victims had been forced to work for scam operations by criminal syndicates and were rescued from imprisonment in a residential compound,” Meta wrote Tuesday. “The victims were malnourished and subjected to both physical and psychological abuses by their captors, who were arrested and are facing prosecution.”

The scam network used various tactics to lure victims into giving money, according to Meta and prosecutors. This included persuading victims into fraudulent investment schemes, offering fake employee opportunities or digital tasks, or posing as law enforcement, military or government officials. It also involved criminals building fake romantic or professional relationships to lure victims into sending money.

Law enforcement agencies from Australia, Canada, India and New Zealand, as well as Interpol, assisted in the investigation.

“Fraud is a global problem and it takes partnership working across international boundaries to tackle it,” Nick Sharp, NCA deputy director of fraud, said in the DOJ’s press release.

“Hosting such a rich and dedicated team of law enforcement and technology companies at NCA’s headquarters enabled us to utilize the power of partnerships and strike back at a significant set of criminals who inflict misery on thousands of victims of fraud.”

articles.body:
Cleveland to be home of next submarine repair center

President Trump announced late Monday that a new “massive” submarine repair center will be in Cleveland, Ohio.

“I’m pleased to announce that the Department of War has officially selected the new home of the U.S. Submarine Component Repair Center, a big deal that everybody wanted and it’s going to be right here in Ohio , in Cleveland, Ohio,” the president said during his rally in Youngstown.

The 46,000 square-foot factory will manufacture, repair and maintain submarine components, White House press secretary Katie Zacharia said on Tuesday.

“Northeast Ohio has the skilled workforce, infrastructure and strategic location to support this critical mission for our U.S. Navy. This facility will strengthen our national security, support military readiness and create jobs in Cleveland,” Sen. Jon Husted (R-Ohio) said in a statement on Tuesday.

“I urged the administration to bring this facility to Northeast Ohio, and I’m proud to see Cleveland selected as its home,” Husted said. “I’ll continue fighting for projects that strengthen our nation’s defense and create opportunities for Ohio workers.”

Back in August, the president put a memo directing administration officials to find a location for the facility within 90 days.

No other details have been released by the administration about the facility.

articles.title: Plataforma de apostas é condenada após bloquear resgate de R$ 51 mil | G1
articles.standfirst: Empresa alegou que aposta estava relacionada a partida na Romênia investigada por suspeita de manipulação, mas não apontou provas. Justiça considerou conduta abusiva.
articles.summary: Empresa alegou que aposta estava relacionada a partida na Romênia investigada por suspeita de manipulação, mas não apontou provas. Justiça considerou conduta abusiva.
articles.body:
Acesso bloqueado Brasil Sem Bets bets site celular — Foto: Isabela Ortiz/g1

Uma plataforma de apostas, que não teve o nome divulgado, foi condenada pela Justiça do Rio Grande do Norte após bloquear o acesso à conta de uma cliente que tinha R$ 51 mil de saldo retidos há um ano e dois meses.

Além de devolver o acesso ao valor, o Juizado Especial Cível e Criminal da Comarca de Apodi , na Região Oeste do estado, determinou ainda o pagamento de R$ 2 mil por danos morais.

Segundo os autos, a consumidora possuía o saldo de R$ 51.365,00 disponível para saque na plataforma, mas teve a conta suspensa e a função de retirada bloqueada quando solicitou o resgate do dinheiro.

Na ação judicial, a cliente afirmou ter procurado a empresa por meio de canais de atendimento, sem conseguir o desbloqueio ou a restituição dos valores.

A empresa alegou na Justiça que o bloqueio se deu de forma preventiva porque a aposta estava relacionada a uma partida de futebol da Liga 3 da Romênia que era investigada por suspeita de manipulação de resultados.

Segundo a empresa, o bloqueio foi realizado como medida de prevenção a fraudes e de integridade esportiva.

Ao analisar o caso, o juiz Fábio Ferreira Vasconcelos entendeu que os documentos apresentados pela plataforma apontavam apenas movimentações consideradas atípicas no mercado daquela partida, sem demonstrar qualquer ligação da consumidora com atletas, clubes, árbitros ou um esquema de manipulação de resultados .

O magistrado destacou sentença que as plataformas de apostas podem adotar medidas de prevenção a fraudes, mas essa providência não permite a retenção indefinida do dinheiro dos usuários.

O valor permaneceu bloqueado por mais de 14 meses e, segundo a Justiça, sem conclusão em prazo razoável e sem informações claras à consumidora . A setença reforçou que essa foi considerada uma conduta abusiva , utilizando como base os artigos 39 e 51 do Código de Defesa do Consumidor.

Para o magistrado, a retenção prolongada de uma quantia significativa, somada às tentativas frustradas de solucionar o problema administrativamente, ultrapassou um simples descumprimento contratual e provocou angústia, sensação de impotência e perda injustificada de tempo . Por isso, ele determinou o retorno à conta e o pagamento de danos morais.

articles.title: Justice Department says North Koreans have infiltrated dozens of U.S. companies | TechCrunch
articles.summary: U.S. authorities warn that sanctioned hackers are increasingly targeting Americans to act as facilitators between breached U.S. companies and Pyongyang.
articles.body:
The U.S. Department of Justice is warning that hackers working for the North Korean regime are increasingly relying on Americans to facilitate the hacking of U.S. companies.

In an announcement on Tuesday, prosecutors said they have indicted and arrested at least two people, and conducted searches across dozens of suspected “laptop farms” in Texas. The computers were allegedly used by North Koreans to remotely hack into American companies and steal sensitive data.

According to the DOJ, federal authorities seized over 180 computers that they believe American companies had shipped out to their newly hired employees, not realizing that they were sanctioned North Korean spies who had used stolen identities of U.S. citizens to gain employment. The DOJ said that it raided over 40 laptop farms across Texas, the largest disclosed number of homes and residences used for facilitating North Korean hacks, which were owned by at least two American facilitators.

CrowdStrike, which helped the FBI investigate and disrupt the latest North Korean operations, said that laptop farms are “vital” to North Korea in helping its hackers overcome physical, financial, and legal challenges of not physically being in the United States.

The prosecutors said at least 70 U.S.-based companies had been infiltrated by the hackers, who are believed to have generated around $3 million in stolen funds. The DOJ did not name the affected companies, but described them as healthcare, cyber support, retail, communications, and manufacturing sectors across Ohio and 16 other states, including the District of Columbia.

“Increasingly, North Korean IT workers are turning to recruiting American facilitators to counter improved private sector detections and law enforcement actions. These workers are hiring facilitators to complete a wider variety of tasks, and in some cases subcontracting entire jobs to third-party foreign nationals,” the Justice Department said .

Oftentimes, North Korean hackers use real-looking email addresses, spoofed LinkedIn profiles, and extensive online and social media accounts as cover for their activities.

In a separate public service announcement , the FBI said that there are “thousands” of North Korean-state controlled IT workers working at Western companies, which “pose a significant national security and intellectual property theft insider threat.”

This is the latest wave of arrests, indictments, and enforcement action targeting North Korean activities in the United States in recent years. The breakaway regime has used this “remote IT workers” scheme to allow North Koreans to gain employment with U.S. and European companies, earn a wage, and then steal sensitive information and intellectual property while as employees. The victim companies are then extorted into paying the hackers further.

The remote IT workers’ scheme is one of several strands of illicit revenue that the North Korean regime aims to generate, including hacking crypto exchanges and open-source developer projects , with the aim of funding its internationally sanctioned nuclear weapons program. The regime is thought to have stolen at least $2 billion in crypto during 2025 alone.

Experts on North Korea have put the number of hacked companies and the amount of stolen crypto as likely much higher than reported.

Earlier this year, CrowdStrike said in a separate report that North Korean hackers were behind around half of all documented “hands-on-keyboard” intrusions over the past year, referring to hacks that are carried out by humans and not automated tools or AI.

articles.title: Zoho founder Sridhar Vembu says AI has made coding faster, but it has not yet …
articles.summary: Zoho founder Sridhar Vembu said that AI is making software development faster, but it has not yet made the process 10 or 100 times more productive.
articles.body: Zoho founder Sridhar Vembu said that AI is making software development faster, but it has not yet made the process 10 or 100 times more productive. Sharing a post on X (formerly Twitter), Vembu said that such a leap could happen in the future, putting pressure on software jobs. “As of today, AI led productivity gain in software development estimates are (at best) 25% to 50% as measured on an end to end product basis (prototyping is much much faster now but finished product requires a lot more human work),” he said in the post adding “A 10x or 100x productivity leap could happen (I believe it will happen, see below) but it has not happened _yet_”.Sridhar Vembu: AI is increasing costs for software companiesIn the post, Sridhar Vembu also pointed to three major expenses that companies are incurring because of AI. These include:“a) server/memory and hardware prices are way up (4-5x in a year for servers) driven by the monster AI data center build out.b) AI token spending per engineer is way up (those productivity gains are costly!)c) Hosting open weight models needs expensive GPUs.”“Layered on top of that is the geopolitical uncertainty. As one example, the Middle East is a major market and the prolonged war is not good. The US stock market is in a monster bubble and it is a mistake to think of stock prices as indicative of future prosperity - the GFC of 2008-9, dotcom bust of 2001-2 as wall as the 1980s Japan bubble all demonstrate that point,” Vembu added.Sridhar Vembu: 10x productivity leap in software is comingVembu says that the 10x productivity leap in software is coming “because of what is happening in the mathematics world. The crucial link is auto-formalization, or formal verification of code. Mathematics theorems are formalized in Lean and proofs are verified by the Lean verifier - Lean is a programming language”.“LLMs do not verify the proof, they generate it to be verified by the Lean verifier and once you have the advanced reasoning capable LLM and Lean verifier in a feedback loop and give plenty of compute, magic happens,” he said.He also shared an analogy explaining how formal automated verification mechanism is coming to LLM generated software. “The analogy is handloom weaving vs powerful machine looms of code,” he wrote.Concluding the post, Vembu wrote “So it is the combination of current data center/AI costs, geopolitical uncertainty and the potential of a 10x or bigger leap in software productivity driven by advances in automatic program verification. These are all challenges to software jobs, and that is why we have called for reinvention internally”.You use AI every day. Now get your AI Quotient. Take the AIQ test.

articles.title: Ukraine showed Trump how easily an enemy could cripple an AI powerhouse
articles.summary: Ukraine's drone attacks on three Yandex data centers in four days exposed how adversaries can cripple artificial intelligence without defeating software.
articles.body: An adversary can interrupt an artificial intelligence system without defeating its software. It need only strike the infrastructure that keeps the system running. Ukraine proved the point inside Russia this past week. President Trump and his national security team should take note before an enemy tries the same thing here. On October 8, a Ukrainian drone attack forced Yandex, the technology company often called "Russia’s Google," to suspend operations at its Sasovo data center. The next day, another strike knocked out several modules at its Kaluga facility, which Yandex had called its most powerful data center in Russia. On October 11, the company announced that its Vladimir-region data center had shut down completely after a drone attack. Ukraine disrupted three major Yandex computing facilities in four days. The Sasovo facility housed two of Yandex’s three supercomputers used to train its AI models, including YandexGPT. Yandex said it could not yet determine whether the equipment could be restored. Whatever the final damage assessment, Russia’s leading AI developer lost a major computing hub in a single night. AMERICA MUST DEFEND OUR DIGITAL INFRASTRUCTURE, HERE AND OVERSEAS, TO WIN THE NEXT WAR During my years as an Army officer and Pentagon strategist, I learned to judge a military capability by whether it would be there when needed. A weapon that dazzles on the test range becomes a liability when its supply line fails in combat. That standard should govern our dependence on AI. The word "cloud" hides the physical machinery behind computing services. Those services require buildings, processors, electricity, cooling equipment and communications networks. The Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency calls energy and communications "fundamental to the operation of practically every other critical infrastructure sector." THE AI REVOLUTION WILL GO WHEREVER THERE'S ELECTRICITY — AND CHINA KNOWS IT That vulnerability reaches well beyond Russia. Government missions, essential services and American businesses all run on advanced computing. When a privately operated facility supports an indispensable defense or intelligence function, its continued availability becomes a national security concern. That does not mean Washington should take these facilities over. A government nameplate on the gate would not stop a single drone. What matters is who defends these sites and how quickly they recover. An outage need not destroy equipment to cause serious harm. Intelligence that arrives after a commander must act may come too late to protect troops or shape the decision. A recovery plan that misses the mission’s deadline is no plan at all. US MILITARY BASES ARE ‘ILL-EQUIPPED’ TO STOP DRONE SWARMS, TOP COMMANDER REVEALS AFTER RUBIO'S UAP WARNING Russia is a war zone, and America is not. But consider Loudoun County, Virginia, which has the highest concentration of data centers in the world, and neighboring Prince William County. Fences, cameras and guards protect those campuses on the ground. None of that stops a drone, and federal law reserves the authority to bring one down for federal agencies and certified state and local police. Ukraine’s strikes give Washington every reason to test whether our essential computing would survive an attack from the air. President Trump has already laid a policy foundation. His June 5 national security memorandum directed agencies to form partnerships with willing private companies to secure America’s most advanced AI technologies. It specifically contemplated threat intelligence sharing, joint AI red-team exercises and stronger physical and cybersecurity protections for the nation’s data centers. The memorandum gave agencies 120 days to develop those partnerships, a deadline that passed on October 3. The administration should now report what it has accomplished: which partnerships are operating, what protections they provide and whether essential missions can continue after a major facility becomes unavailable. Trump’s new Super Intelligence Task Force, announced October 4 and led by Director of National Intelligence Jay Clayton, is the right venue to demand those answers. Reuters reported October 8 that vice chair Scott Kupor expected the full committee to convene this week and to issue a charter afterward. Infrastructure readiness belongs in that charter. The president should direct four practical steps. First, identify the computing capabilities essential to national defense, intelligence and other indispensable government missions. Assess the cost of losing them, the availability of alternatives and the time required to restore operations. The mission, not a facility’s price tag or size, should determine its security priority. Second, assign responsibility. Private operators must harden their facilities and build redundancy. Defending the airspace above them is government’s job, so federal agencies and local police should plan counter-drone coverage for the most critical sites. Federal agencies must also provide timely threat information, define requirements for the missions they purchase and coordinate emergency assistance. The president should name a single official responsible for pulling those efforts together and closing gaps. Third, establish proportionate, enforceable security requirements. Government contracts can require protection and continuity arrangements for essential services, and Congress should close demonstrated gaps in authority. Requirements should cover power, cooling and communications as well as computing equipment. Fourth, test recovery the way Washington-area agencies have long exercised their continuity of operations plans in drills such as FEMA’s annual Eagle Horizon. Those tests should include the loss of more than one facility or a shared power or communications provider. Can another site accept the workload? Are the necessary data, equipment and personnel available? Can operations resume within the mission’s deadline? Where the answer is no, fix it before a crisis. Congress should receive classified reports on those results. A public summary can establish accountability without revealing sensitive facilities or defensive measures. The civilian nuclear industry offers a useful precedent. The Nuclear Regulatory Commission requires nuclear power plants to maintain armed security officers, physical barriers and intrusion detection, and it tests those defenses with force-on-force exercises. Most of those plants are privately owned. AI data centers pose different hazards, and Washington should not copy nuclear rules wholesale. The principle carries over: private ownership and enforceable federal security obligations can coexist. America should preserve the entrepreneurship that drives technological progress while requiring dependable service for essential national missions. Targeted protections can deliver both. The larger danger lies in the Pacific. In any conflict with China, America will need computing power that survives the first blow. Washington should identify how an adversary would try to knock that capacity out and require defenses and recovery plans proven in exercises. CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP Ukraine’s strikes are a warning shot. President Trump should demand a tested answer to the question they raise: When a critical American AI facility goes down, can our essential missions continue?

articles.title: Rolex and Gold Were for US and Not Trump, Swiss Trade Chief Says
articles.summary: Gifts presented to President Donald Trump by Swiss executives were actually for the American people, according to Bern’s top trade diplomat.
articles.body:
(Bloomberg) -- Gifts presented to President Donald Trump by Swiss executives were actually for the American people, according to Bern's top trade diplomat.

In an interview on Wednesday at the Bloomberg New Economy Forum in New Delhi, Secretary of State and head of SECO Helene Budliger Artieda told Francine Lacqua that handing over a Rolex table clock and engraved gold bar at the White House wasn't illegal.

"It's a gift to the American people — it's duly registered at the White House, and if all things go well it will end up in a presidential library," she said. "It's a private-sector initiative, but I feel confident that they have kept within the margins of the law."

The items delivered in the Oval Office last November by a business delegation seeking relief from Trump's onerous tariffs became a matter of national controversy in Switzerland.

Lawmakers filed criminal complaints seeking a probe for possible bribery, and a parliamentary report on the matter is expected in due course.

"I've been assured by these business leaders that they had their compliance look into it," Budliger said. "The Swiss government didn't gift anything. I think that's the most important thing."

The unusual appeal to Trump last year followed the imposition of 39% tariffs. Budliger was a key player behind the scenes to secure an accord that capped levies at 15%.

"The US has respected that deal," Budliger said. "We want to have certainty, we want to have calmer waters."

Talks are still ongoing to secure a more permanent legally binding agreement, she said.

"Sticking to being calm and cool-headed and seeing how we can make this relationship win-win has helped us to then get to a 15-all-in percent deal," she said.

With assistance from Bastian Benrath-Wright.

articles.title: Musk steps back into politics with redefined DC role
articles.summary: Elon Musk is jumping back into the political fray, reviving his role as a massive election spender and technology leader with a seat at the table again in Washington. Following a brief hiatus from President Trump’s orbit last year, Musk’s latest appearances in D.C. and influx of election cash signal he still has an appetite…
articles.body:
Elon Musk is jumping back into the political fray, reviving his role as a massive election spender and technology leader with a seat at the table again in Washington.

Following a brief hiatus from President Trump’s orbit last year, Musk’s latest appearances in D.C. and influx of election cash signal he still has an appetite for politics and policy involvement.

Despite suggesting earlier this year he could pull back his political involvement, Musk’s recent election spending makes him the largest campaign donor of 2026 as he tries to give Republicans a boost ahead of the midterms.

And while he isn’t serving as Trump’s adviser anymore, he is increasingly appearing alongside the president at high-stakes events and took on a new leadership role for a Pentagon project .

“Nothing brings people together like a common enemy and it’s election season,” GOP strategist Chris Johnson told The Hill.

Musk’s uptick in spending made headlines Monday, when a spokesperson for his America PAC confirmed the technology executive gave $276 million to several Republican super PACs and organizations over the past three months.

The latest donations, first reported by The New York Times , bring Musk’s contributions to $366 million this election cycle.

“If Democrats take control of Washington and win key gubernatorial and attorney general races this November, then America risks becoming a socialist, woke and borderless country,” Andrew Romeo, a spokesperson for America PAC, said in a statement to the Times confirmed by The Hill.

“These robust investments have allowed the GOP apparatus to get its message out so Republicans can have a fighting chance to defy history,” Romeo added.

With less than a month before the midterm elections, Republicans are facing an uphill battle to keep their razor-thin majorities in Congress. The nation’s top election analysts have shifted projections for dozens of House seats in recent weeks, almost all in Democrats’ favor.

“He is analyzing the political climate right now, and he sees that he can have an impact,” Brendan Steinhauser, a Texas-based Republican strategist and CEO of the Alliance for Secure AI, said, adding, “if you ask most Republicans” about Musk’s donations, “it would be welcome.”

After years of staying out of politics, Musk quickly became one of the Republican Party’s top supporters in the 2024 election, pouring hundreds of millions of dollars into Trump’s reelection campaign.

He joined the then-candidate on the trail and later led Trump’s cost-cutting effort known as the Department of Government Efficiency (DOGE), becoming a near-constant presence at Mar-a-Lago, Cabinet meetings and the Oval Office.

While Trump and Musk stood behind DOGE’s mission, the project drew controversy across many months for its sweeping job and funding cuts across the federal government.

Musk departed the White House in late May 2025 on what seemed like good terms after his special government employee status expired, but days later, he and Trump clashed in a public blowout, ending — at least temporarily — their close alliance.

In the aftermath it was unclear how Musk felt about the GOP, and at one point, the billionaire tried to launch a third party . He eventually paused plans for this, stepped away from politics and returned focus to his various tech ventures.

Musk, the richest person in the world, said last May he planned to spend “ a lot less ” on politics and later told The Economist in July he “ got carried away ” and “a little too involved in politics.”

However, later that month, Musk authorized America PAC to spend $100 million to $120 million for a field program focused on conservative voter turnout in the 2026 midterms.

“Elon realizes that he has a team. … For better or worse, the Republicans are that team,” Johnson said. “The folks in the White House are friendly with the tech industry, and they’re really underrating just how hostile a Democratic majority, especially if they take the Senate, will be to Big Tech.”

“Elon is doing the correct calculation that he needs to make sure that the folks that have been on this team and have his back, even if there was a momentary fallout, that he needs to remind them that, and himself, that they’re all on the same team,” Johnson added.

The baggage of DOGE and his blowout with Trump do not seem to be stopping Musk from reshaping a role in Washington.

“There were critics of course of his actions at [DOGE], but I think generally the DOGE stuff is still a net positive for Republicans or at least a neutral,” Steinhauser said.

On Musk’s past feud with Trump, Stephen Myrow, managing partner at Beacon Policy Advisors, suggested Musk’s return to the president’s orbit follows the same pattern with the commander in chief.

Trump “tends to have a lot of tumultuous relationships, we refer to it as Trump’s ever-evolving orbit, where people go in the orbit, and they’re the shiny new toy, and then they have a falling-out and they land in the penalty box,” Myrow told The Hill.

“A lot of times, months later, these guys come out of the penalty box. It depends on how big the break is, and if there’s, in a transactional way, any value, and obviously Elon presents value,” he added.

While Musk’s brief stint at the White House focused on overhauling the federal government, his recent moves show he’s largely focused on science and technology in D.C.

Musk, alongside Anduril co-founder Palmer Luckey and former Speaker Newt Gingrich (R-Ga.), was tapped to lead a new Pentagon effort to study the future of warfare, dubbed “Project Meridian.”

According to Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth, Musk, Luckey and Gingrich — under the leadership of Emil Michael, undersecretary of Defense for research and engineering — will focus on discovering weapons and systems for “any future battlefield.”

Trump also appears to be turning to Musk for tech expertise and guidance. The tech mogul sat directly next to Trump for his AI luncheon last month with numerous other CEOs, and the president later awarded him the National Medal of Science.

The tech mogul was also one of a handful of tech executives who sat at the president’s table for the state dinner with Chinese President Xi Jinping.

“What we’re seeing now is just [Musk] doing what his expertise is and offering that as his expertise rather than just being, I think what a lot of people would argue, a necessary sledgehammer to a very fine-tuned machine, but he’s much more designed and built for this kind of stuff,” Johnson said.

images.caption: President Donald Trump, right, presents the National Medal of Science to Elon Musk at the U.S. Institute of Peace, Thursday, Oct. 8, 2026, in Washington. (AP Photo/Julia Demaree Nikhinson)

articles.title: Trump, Vance signal unease with Hegseth’s public execution plan
articles.summary: The White House has signalled a potential reversal of course after Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth announced plans to livestream the firing squad execution of former Army Maj. Nidal Hasan, the 2009 Fort Hood shooter, prompting bipartisan outcry. President Trump has publicly sent mixed signals on the plan, while privately telling one confidant it “might not…
articles.body:
The White House has signalled a potential reversal of course after Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth announced plans to livestream the firing squad execution of former Army Maj. Nidal Hasan, the 2009 Fort Hood shooter, prompting bipartisan outcry.

President Trump has publicly sent mixed signals on the plan, while privately telling one confidant it “might not happen,” Axios reported Monday .

Trump has given his enthusiastic endorsement for executing Hasan by firing squad, but said he “wasn’t involved in that decision” to livestream the Dec. 3 execution.

On Saturday, Trump told reporters he would “make a decision ultimately” on what to do.

“There are two thoughts: Don’t show it and show it, because you know by showing it, maybe other people won’t be doing what he did,” the president said. “So I’ll make a decision ultimately. I know what the military would like to do, but we’ll make a decision.”

Asked on Tuesday whether he had decided, Trump replied, “We’re looking at it.”

Hasan killed 13 people and injured 32 others when he opened fire at Fort Hood, Texas, in November 2009. The incident is the deadliest mass shooting on a U.S. military installation.

Vice President Vance offered a more definite tone when he told reporters Friday he will not watch the execution should it be livestreamed, even stating, “I don’t know that that’s actually going to happen.”

And House Speaker Mike Johnson (R-La.), a top defender of the administration, said he would not watch such a livestream and intended to warn the White House against the idea.

“The concern would be that it would create a video that would be a recruiting tool for future terrorists,” Johnson said in a CBS News interview that aired over the weekend, adding, “I need to tell the White House what some of my colleagues think about that, and not everybody’s in favor of the idea.”

The comments, taken together, reflect a deep unease inside and outside the administration over Hegseth’s plan, even as they support the death sentence.

Hegseth first announced the idea Wednesday aboard the USS Abraham Lincoln in San Diego, telling far-right podcaster Jack Posobiec: “We’ll make sure that people are able to watch it, that it’s public, because people need to understand that there’s serious consequences for these types of things.”

Within the Army and Pentagon, the news came as a surprise to many, with questions still swirling as to how and where the execution would be livestreamed, given there are regulations about who can watch a military execution.

Also unclear is which soldiers would be selected to fire on Hasan, as well as the optics around showing the firing squad death of an immobilized 56-year-old man in a wheelchair. Hasan was paralyzed in the Fort Hood shooting when others, seeking to neutralize him, shot him four times.

Lawmakers from both sides of the aisle decried the idea as beneath American values and akin to public executions in authoritarian nations, such as Iran and North Korea. They also warned it could inspire extremists or turn the convicted mass murderer into a martyr.

Sen. Lisa Murkowski (R-Alaska) on Friday urged Hegseth to reverse the decision, writing on the social platform X she “would expect this from terrorists and dictators, but not here in America.”

Sen. Thom Tillis (R-N.C.) has called the plan “beyond disgusting,” while Rep. Austin Scott (R-Ga.) said livestreaming executions “is what jihadists do.”

And Sen. Kevin Cramer (R-N.D.) echoed Johnson’s warning that the livestream could fuel radicalization.

Even survivors of the Fort Hood shooting have questioned Hegseth’s decision to livestream Hasan’s death.

Julia Wilson, a former Defense Department civilian employee, told Fox News Digital on Monday that she wants to be there when the convicted shooter is executed, but worries about broadcasting it.

“I’m kind of shocked that they’re going to go so far as to televise it,” said Wilson. “Unfortunately, some children may end up seeing that, that don’t need to see something like that.”

Sgt. Alonzo Lunsford, who was shot seven times in the Fort Hood attack, said Monday on NewsNation’s Katie Pavlich Tonight that while he’s “excited about the firing squad,” he has an issue with children potentially seeing it.

“The young minds are not in a position to process seeing a horrific act,” Lunsford said. “It’s not for everybody’s eyes. It’s not a thing where we’re going to have a tailgate. . .. Because as a country, as a people, we’re better than that.”

Department of Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin appears to be one of the few administration officials to support a livestream killing, telling CBS News’s “Face the Nation” on Sunday that “no one has to watch it” and that Trump is “restoring American values.”

Should Hasan be executed in December, it would mark the military’s first execution in six decades.

images.caption: Media film in preparation of the start of the court-martial of Maj. Nidal Malik Hasan, Aug. 6, 2013, in Fort Hood, Texas.

articles.title: Pentagon taps DOD public affairs official as Stars and Stripes publisher
articles.summary: The Pentagon has appointed a Department of Defense (DOD) public affairs official as the acting publisher of the military newspaper Stars and Stripes weeks after firing three staffers at the independent publication for what it called subordination. The DOD named Chris Devine, a former Marine Corps colonel, as the acting publisher of the news outlet,…
articles.body:
The Pentagon has appointed a Department of Defense (DOD) public affairs official as the acting publisher of the military newspaper Stars and Stripes weeks after firing three staffers at the independent publication for what it called subordination.

The DOD named Chris Devine, a former Marine Corps colonel, as the acting publisher of the news outlet, the Pentagon chief spokesperson Sean Parnell told The Hill in a late Tuesday statement.

Parnell said Devine, who was the executive director and principal adviser for public affairs policy, proponency and programs within the department’s public affairs office, brings “unmatched expertise, strategic vision, and a commitment to ensuring Stars and Stripes maintains editorial independence while delivering exclusive, mission-focused reporting that directly serves America’s warfighters and their families.”

“In this interim role, he will provide decisive leadership to modernize Stars and Stripes and to strengthen its mission,” Parnell said.

The appointment raises questions about the newspaper’s independence , as the Stars and Stripes is owned and partially funded by DOD but has historically enjoyed editorial freedom.

Devine, however, said he is committed to maintaining the news outlet’s independence from the Pentagon.

“I am confident that Stripes can modernize its platform to prioritize original reporting and content that is relevant and unique to the U.S. military community and not typically covered by commercial media,” Devine told Stars and Stripes.

Devine’s new role comes after the Pentagon fired the Stars and Stripes publisher, Max Lederer, Editor-in-Chief Erik Slavin and reporter Lara Korte in August. DOD directed the long-time publisher to present separation notices to Korte and Slavin, charging the two with insubordination for comments made during a “CBS Sunday Morning” interview.

The trio sued the Pentagon in federal court , alleging the firings were violations of DOD’s own personnel rules and the First Amendment.

The Pentagon removed Jacqueline Smith, the newspaper’s ombudsman, in April. Smith, who later sued over her removal, was tasked with overseeing the news outlet’s editorial independence and reporting concerns to Congress.

The Pentagon has looked to take over the editorial control of the newspaper and refocus coverage on “warfighting” and get rid of “woke distractions .”

The Pentagon has also named Navy Capt. William Urban deputy publisher of the newspaper, a decision that prompted concerns among some Democrats in Congress.

The same day Lederer, Slavin and Korte were fired, DOD put out new guidance for Stars and Stripes, stating the outlet will maintain “editorial operations independent of the military chain of command, military public affairs activities, or other external influences, free from censorship or propaganda,” but has to “safeguard information by preventing the disclosure of classified information and controlled unclassified information and by avoiding the publication of material that would adversely affect national security or clearly endanger U.S. personnel.”

articles.title: Hotter-than-expected inflation report puts prospect of October rate hike back in play
articles.summary: Markets were not yet pricing in a likelihood that the Fed hikes rates later this month on the back of the hotter-than-expected CPI report.
articles.body:
Inflation heated back up in September, putting the prospect of an interest rate hike this month back on the table as Federal Reserve officials consider the extent and timing of future hikes.

The Consumer Price Index rose 3.7% in September , compared with expectations for 3.6%, and an acceleration from 3.4% in August. Month-over-month prices rose 0.6%, versus expectations for 0.5%. Stripping out volatile food and energy prices — the way the Fed likes to scrutinize underlying inflation — CPI rose 0.3% month over month, compared with expectations for 0.2%, holding the same level as August. The year-over-year rate was 2.6%, compared with expectations for 2.5%, and up from 2.4% in August.

A big surge in gas prices accounted for over half of the increase. Gas prices rose 9.1% in September, while the energy index as a whole increased 5.2% following a 2.1% increase in August.

Markets were not yet pricing in the likelihood that the Fed will hike rates later this month on the back of the hotter-than-expected CPI report. According to CME Group, traders see just a 43.7% chance of a quarter-point hike later this month, up from about 20% before the inflation report. However, the yield on the 10-year Treasury ( ^TNX ) was moving higher, cresting above 5.3% on Wednesday morning. Markets are pricing in better than 50% odds that the central bank hikes rates for a second time this year in December.

"The upside surprise to core CPI in September was broad-based rather than due to any obvious temporary factors, therefore bringing an October rate hike back into play and presenting upside risks to our forecast for just two more 25 bp hikes from the Fed," said Stephen Brown, chief North America economist for Capital Economics.

A chorus of Fed officials has been calling for further rate hikes to bring down inflation , which has remained above the Fed's 2% target for over five years, while leaving flexibility on when those hikes might occur.

"If the economic data continue to come in as expected, I anticipate additional hikes to support a timelier return of inflation to our 2% goal," Fed governor Chris Waller said earlier this month. "But there is some flexibility about when those hikes will occur. The hikes do not need to come at consecutive meetings, but they should be in place in an acceptable period of time."

The Boston Fed's Susan Collins said Tuesday that it would "be appropriate to raise rates a bit further before the end of the year to ensure a timely and durable return of inflation" to the Fed's 2 percent target. She too said the timing would depend on the data.

articles.title: Watch live: Hegseth talks future of autonomous warfare amid leadership shake-ups
articles.summary: Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth is set to discuss the future of autonomous warfare Wednesday morning as the Pentagon pushes to modernize the military amid leadership shake-ups. Hegseth will join acting Army Secretary Adam Telle and acting Navy Secretary Hung Cao at the Association of the United States Army’s annual meeting for a discussion on Project…
articles.body:
Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth is set to discuss the future of autonomous warfare Wednesday morning as the Pentagon pushes to modernize the military amid leadership shake-ups.

Hegseth will join acting Army Secretary Adam Telle and acting Navy Secretary Hung Cao at the Association of the United States Army’s annual meeting for a discussion on Project Agincourt , focused on unmanned systems.

The appearance comes a day after acting Army chief of staff Gen. Christopher LaNeve insisted the service is “sprinting” toward modernization despite recent leadership changes.

Hegseth also faces questions over costs associated with the ongoing Iran war and bipartisan backlash over his proposal to livestream the execution of convicted Fort Hood shooter Nidal Hasan.

The event is scheduled to begin at 10 a.m. EDT.

articles.title: Judge orders Trump administration to halt work at DC golf course until later this month
articles.summary: A federal judge on Tuesday ordered the Trump administration to stop work on East Potomac Park, site of East Potomac Golf Links and a property the president has been eyeing for redevelopment. U.S. District Judge Ana Reyes’ order came after hundreds of trees were cut down at the property over the weekend. The action marks…
articles.body:
A federal judge on Tuesday ordered the Trump administration to stop work on East Potomac Park , site of East Potomac Golf Links and a property the president has been eyeing for redevelopment.

U.S. District Judge Ana Reyes’ order came after hundreds of trees were cut down at the property over the weekend. The action marks an apparent violation of a previous order requiring the Department of Interior and National Parks Service to notify the court and preservationist groups suing to stop the project before carrying out any further work.

Reyes ordered no more tree cutting or landscaping can be conducted before Oct. 28, as she considered the lawsuit which accuses the Trump administration of attempting to revamp public lands for the president’s personal wishes.

Trump has long eyed the property, which for years has been home to a number of public golf courses, walking trails and gathering spaces for residents and tourists alike.

The National Links Trust, the non-profit that has overseen the courses since the COVID-19 pandemic, announced a deal with the Trump administration earlier this year for the Interior Department to overhaul the property with a major renovation.

The president has enlisted the help of leading golf course architect Tom Fazio’s firm with the project. He said the move would lead to East Potomac being transformed into an 18-hole championship style facility capable of hosting professional tournaments and future Ryder Cups.

East Potomac is known around the country as a model for affordable public golf, catering in many cases to junior and beginner golfers.

The next hearing in the lawsuit seeking to stop the project is slated for Monday.

images.caption: Golfers drive a cart past cut down trees and piles of wood chips at the East Potomac Golf Links, Monday, Oct. 12, 2026, in Washington. (AP Photo/Mark Schiefelbein)
